name: Sticker Types
h1: Types of Die Cut Stickers, Decals and Labels
seoTitle: Sticker Types Explained: Die Cut Decals, Labels & Holographic
seoDescription: Die cut decals, die cut labels and holographic die cut stickers compared: construction, where each belongs, and how to choose between the three.
tagline: Sticker, decal and label are not the same thing. This page sorts the types so the product you order matches the job.
quickAnswer: The main custom sticker types are printed stickers (ink on a face film with a backing), decals (a graphic transferred to a surface, often cut vinyl with no printed background), and labels (stickers made for product identification, usually on rolls or sheets). Each is available die cut to the artwork outline, in holographic, vinyl or paper, from $0.30 per piece.

sections.h2: Sticker, decal or label: a working definition
sections.html:
Printers use the three words loosely, and so do customers, which is how a bakery ends up with a box of vehicle-grade decals when it needed roll labels. The distinctions that matter are construction and purpose. A sticker is any printed piece with adhesive on the back. A decal is a graphic meant to be transferred onto a surface and read as part of it: a van door, a storefront window, a helmet. A label identifies or describes a product and usually ships in a format that suits a packing bench. The same vinyl can be all three; the cut, the backing and the quantity change.

The long version, with photos of each construction, is in our guide to die cut stickers versus decals versus labels.

sections.h2: Die cut decals for surfaces that are part of the message
sections.html: A decal is judged by how well it disappears into the surface. On a vehicle that means cast vinyl that conforms to rivets and curves, a matte or gloss laminate that matches the paint, and a cut outline with no visible border. On a storefront window it often means a reverse-printed clear decal applied inside the glass so the weather never touches it. Decals are usually bigger than stickers, applied once, and expected to last for years, so the quote leans toward heavier film and a laminate by default. The custom die cut decals page covers transfer tape, wet application and the difference between calendered and cast vinyl.

sections.h2: Die cut labels for products and packaging
sections.html:
Labels are stickers with a job: identify the product, carry the ingredients or barcode, seal the box. They ship on rolls for a dispenser or on sheets for hand application, and they are ordered in larger quantities and reordered on a schedule. Material follows the product: BOPP or vinyl for anything refrigerated or used in a bathroom, paper for dry goods and shipping cartons. Die cutting lets the label follow the panel of the package instead of being a rectangle on a curved jar.

  1. Measure the flat panel of the container, not the whole circumference.
  2. Pick paper for dry shelf products, BOPP or vinyl for wet ones.
  3. Choose rolls if you apply more than a few hundred a week.
  4. Leave a 0.125-inch safe zone inside the cut for text.
  5. Order a 100-piece run and apply it on real containers before scaling up.

Format and material choices are on the die cut labels page, and the packaging-specific version sits under custom packaging labels.

sections.h2: Holographic die cut stickers for merch and limited runs
sections.html: Holographic film gives the strongest reaction of any sticker type on a table at an event or in an unboxing video, which is why it dominates merch drops, record releases and product seals. The diffraction layer sits under the print, so the design needs unprinted areas for the rainbow to show; a fully covered holographic sticker looks like a slightly shiny ordinary one. Simple logos and bold lettering work; fine type and photographs do not. Outdoor life is a little shorter than white vinyl. Holographic die cut stickers are priced on the same square-inch basis as vinyl with a film surcharge.

sections.h2: Choosing a type when your job fits two
sections.html:
When a job sits between types, decide by how it will be applied and how long it must last. A logo for laptops is a sticker; the same logo at 18 inches for a van is a decal; the same logo at 2 inches on 5,000 jars is a label. If you still cannot place it, describe the surface and the quantity on the quote form and we will assign the type, the material and the format for you. Mixed orders are common: one artwork can ship as 500 roll labels, 200 die cut stickers and 2 vehicle decals from one proof.

  • Applied by the customer, one at a time: sticker.
  • Applied once to a large surface: decal.
  • Applied in volume on a packing line: label.
  • Needs shine for a launch or event: holographic die cut.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a sticker and a decal?
faqs.a: A sticker is any printed piece with adhesive and a backing. A decal is a graphic meant to be transferred to a surface and read as part of it, such as a van door or shop window, so it is usually larger, laminated, often supplied with transfer tape and expected to last years.

faqs.q: Are die cut labels and die cut stickers the same product?
faqs.a: Same materials and cutting, different format and purpose. Labels identify a product and ship on rolls or sheets for a packing bench, usually in larger quantities. Stickers ship as individual pieces for hand application. Tell us which you need and we set the format.

faqs.q: What sticker type is best for laptops and water bottles?
faqs.a: A die cut vinyl sticker with a gloss or matte laminate. The laminate protects against scratches and dishwasher cycles, the die cut removes the white border, and 2.5 to 4 inches is the size range that fits a laptop lid or the side of a bottle.

faqs.q: Which sticker type should I use on a vehicle?
faqs.a: A die cut decal on cast vinyl with a laminate. Cast film conforms to curves and does not shrink, and the laminate takes car washes and sun. Calendered vinyl is fine for short-term promotions under a year or for flat trailer panels.

faqs.q: Can holographic die cut stickers be used as product seals?
faqs.a: Yes, and they work well as tamper-evident seals because the film shows any lifting. Keep the design simple, leave at least a quarter of the film unprinted so the shimmer shows, and choose a permanent adhesive so the seal cannot be reapplied cleanly.

Stickers where the blade cuts through the face film but not the backing sheet, so several shapes stay on one sheet and peel off individually. They are the standard format for sticker packs, planner stickers and event giveaways, and they are cheaper per piece than individual die cuts.

faqs.q: Do decals come with transfer tape?
faqs.a: Cut-vinyl decals with separate letters or elements do, so the whole layout transfers in one piece. Printed die cut decals that are a single piece do not need it. Ask on the quote if your decal has loose elements and we include the tape.

faqs.q: Can one artwork be ordered as several sticker types?
faqs.a: Yes, from a single proof. Roll labels for packaging, die cut stickers for giveaways and a couple of large decals for the shop window can be quoted together. Each type has its own 100-piece minimum except large decals, which can be ordered in small numbers.

Kiss cut sheets, then standard-shape paper labels on rolls, then die cut vinyl stickers. Decals cost more because they are larger and on heavier film. Holographic die cut stickers cost the most per square inch because of the film.

faqs.q: How do I know if my design works as a die cut type?
faqs.a: If it has a clear outline, bold shapes and no fine points thinner than a tenth of an inch, it will cut cleanly. Designs with photographic backgrounds or very thin elements are better as circle or rectangle stickers. Send the file and we draw the cut line on the proof.
